blocks.x: So you can give your name first. All right.
I am John Lewis Bruma's trumpet player of New Orleans. It's loud enough, isn't it?
Yeah, that's fine. All right. Give your birthday.
Okay, we were going on about your life, about when you started.
Yeah, that's right, when I started. Well, like I said, Willie Humphrey was actually my first teacher.
What kind of a horn did you have? A hornet or a hornet?
I had a trumpet. And I forget, I bought that trumpet from Morris, how do you pronounce the name? Coloskey or? I don't know. Morris Music Shop was on Rampall Street.
That was the Morris Music Shop.

Yeah, Morris Coloskey, I think it was something like that was his name. He was a kind of big fat fella. Well, I bought a, how do you call that metal again? Nickel played a trumpet for me, for $60. And that was plenty of money. Oh yeah, that was plenty of money. And I bought that trumpet. Huh? It was a Morris Special. They had written on it, Morris Special. See, well man, I thought the world of that thing. Oh yeah. Oh yeah. See? Well, like I said before, I mean, I didn't accomplish anything with Willie. But technically speaking, I mean, he was, he was my first teacher as far as, as far as that. Because he was the one, I mean, who started me off with the trumpet and everything, you know, and all that kind of rigmarole.
Did he have his teacher with his hornet or what did he teach you with? Did he have any instruments?
Did he have an instrument? Yeah. Let me see if I could.
Or did he have the whole band together at one time?

Well, that is, I mean, all the students gather in the, in the basement like, you know what I mean? And I just can't remember, Woody, if he told us or, or just what he said. But I mean, but, but I mean, I could remember this. I mean, if he had told me, if he had stopped me off that music had five lines in four spaces, I mean, I could remember that. But I don't think he told me that.
Yeah.

You know? When did you first learn to read that? Well, now, that came years and years later. That's right. When I first learned, learned to read. Well, all right. That went on there. So, but then I don't know, something happened and I stopped fooling with the trumpet. See? I remember that distinct. I think my grandfather died. That's how it was. Yeah. My grandfather died. And it was a custom during, during, during those times that you're, you know, you pay strict attention to the dead. I mean, you're.
Three in the morning.

Yeah, the morning, you know, no music or no nothing, you know? So, I mean, well, I couldn't practice the trumpet. So eventually, I mean, I lost interest in, and all that in, in the horn. I got one. I lost interest in, in the horn at the time, which was that, it wasn't that, that much interest at that time either. You know, it was just the mild idea of when I was a kid to show off in front of the older kids. Or the other kids. You know what I mean? Yeah. So, I put that trumpet down a long time.
See?

And, uh, then when I did decide, matter of fact, I even forgot where I put the trumpet at. But we had one of those old time armors with them big high armors. Yeah. And the trumpet was on top of the arm. See? And the armors was almost hitting the ceiling, so quite natural, I couldn't see. You know what I'm saying? And, uh, and I don't know, fumbling around there, and I happened to run, I said, oh, look at my trumpet up here. Then I got the thing down. I mean, boy, they had dust about an inch thick on it, you know? I got it down, and then I started dusting it off, and then I started blowing it again. Okay? So, uh, now how I come to go to Morris Music Shop for lessons, I don't, I don't quite remember that. But anyhow, I went to Morris Music Shop for lessons, and they had an old professor there named Professor Milton. He was, uh, he was an old, uh, uh, I think he was a West Indian, I think. I'll never forget him. I don't remember him good. Professor Milton. Well, he started me, he started me to, to, to learn how to read. And then again, I mean, I wasn't interested in the reading part, because, I mean, I was copying those records so well, you understand? That I said, well, I'm happy to learn how to read. Then I had no one to encourage me to learn how to read. See? So, uh, matter of fact, I had such a good ear that when I used to go to lessons, and I used to see them, them other children that was actually reading, you know, and I'd wash their fingering and all that, you know? And I used to play that same thing and, and, and so I sure was reading, but being truthful with myself, you know? For me, you know, seven and five cents a night. Sometime fifty cents a night. Sometime a dollar a night. See? And if you had the job paid $2 a night, man, that was plenty of money.
Do you remember your very first job?

No, my very first job. I never thought about that. My first job. Where was my first job? You know, I can't think about my really first job. What band might be with the kids that played with you? At that time, no, when I was playing, I used to play with older men. I was playing that good.
Older men?

You know? Yeah. As a matter of fact, I don't know if you all know, Gassum played banjo? I've heard the name. Well, Gassum was the banjo. I was playing with his band at one time, and I think I was about 12 or 13 years old.
That's right, see?

I mean, I was playing that well, I mean, over men, you know? See? But like I said, I mean, I was copying those records. Following behind Louis Armstrong and this guy and that guy, see? But up until today, my favorite trumpet player is Roy Eldridge. That's my favorite, you know? Because my son and I always have a big discussion about Roy Eldridge. He like Dizzy Gillespie, you know? Quite natural. I mean, he's young. I mean, he come up in that stage, you know? To Dizzy Gillespie, see? So we got a record there with Dizzy Gillespie and Roy Eldridge blowing at one another just with a- Oh, yeah. And that's the office. He said, Dad, I want to see if I can get you like that, you know? You and I are going to blow. I said, boy, you better leave me alone, I'm good, you know? Yeah, you better leave me alone. Well, anyhow, let's see. What were I discussing now? You talked about your first job.
Yeah, my first job.

I can't remember my really first job, but I know I was going to school. I was going to Sam's school, I think I was about in the sixth grade or something like that. Sixth grade or the- yeah, something like that. And I used to play a lot on Decatur Street. They had places called Popeye and- oh, different- no, they had a lot of different names around there. And that's where we used to get- some places used to pay 75 cents a night, some places used to pay a dollar a night. During the Depression. During the Depression, oh yeah, very much so during the Depression. That was somewhere around 1931, 32, somewhere else in there, 33, somewhere else along in there it was. See? And, uh, well I mean I used to play a lot of rhyme around it, because that's where most of the white was out that way, see?
More than Bourbon, what? Anything along Bourbon Street that was-

At that time, I don't remember. But I mean I remember that they had the district out there, because I mean I used to walk around there, you know, like a lot of those young boys used to just walk through there. But as far as Bourbon Street, I don't- I don't remember Bourbon Street well at all. I mean until later on, you know. Yeah. See? So, uh, let's see, now I played around- around the- then, uh, at that time the Cal- uh, the- where the Caledonia is now, there used to be Japanese tea garden. Yeah. Well, I used to play there a lot too. There- there used to be a dollar a night, you know? And, uh, I played at the Gypsy Tea Room with Kid Renee, and sometime, uh, uh, and at that time Gypsy Tea Room was running every night. See? But then again, sometime Kid Renee wouldn't show up on a job or something like that, so they hired somebody else, and then somebody else would come and get me, and that's how I got to play with those older fellas like that, you know? Because, uh, uh, if I say it myself, I mean I was playing well in- you know, at that time, you know. See? Because, I mean, you- like I said, I wasn't- I wasn't reading but I was playing off those records and- and uh, and uh, and uh, and especially a young kid, I mean, like I was- was playing all of them things that Lewis Armstrong was playing. his arms don't know what's paying, well that was, yeah, them guys thought that was wonderful, you know? So that's how I come to wake so much, see? And I forget, I mean, I used to, when I was working on Decatur Street there, I used to walk from Decatur and Dumaine. Decatur and Dumaine, I used to walk straight down home, and I'd get home about three, four o'clock in the morning right there, just me and my truck, you know? And one of the other times waking up for school the next day. Yeah, tell my mama, sometimes she didn't want me to go out and play, she said, because I was too hard to wake up. But when I used to come home, I used to bring that dollar home, and oh boy, she did wonders with that dollar, you know what I mean? See? See, of course, I mean, I never had no brothers or no sisters, I mean, I'm the only child. I forgot that I was going to ask. Yeah, that's right, I'm the only child. I didn't have no brothers, no sisters. No sisters. And, well now, after that, let me see, yeah. Somebody had hired me for a job to play with Harold Dejean, which is my cousin. I found it out when I played the job, but I didn't know him, you know? No, I didn't know Harold, see? So I played with Harold and Georgie Parker, play piano. Play piano, he was playing piano, Harold Dejean was playing saxophone. I can't remember the other fellas. So, and that's where Harold, looked like Harold had charge of the job. So, I heard him say, told Georgie Parker, say, who sing them here, you know? That's before we start off, you know? I said, who's sending him here? Send a boy here, man. That boy can't play nothing, you know? So, and, so, Georgie said, man, I don't know who's sending him here. Somebody's sending him here. That was downtown at, at one of those halls. So then he said, well, let's see what he could do, you know? So they struck up some tune, and man, I wear that tune, so they actually started asking my name, you know? And all that. So, I mean, I really did well, you know? So, I told my name, I said, well, I said, well, I told Harold, I said, Harold, I said, I got a cousin that played trumpet too, you know? You said, who's your cousin? I said, Leo Dejean. I said, Leo Dejean? He said, what'd you say your name is? I said, my name is John Brunus. I said, they called me Picky for a nickname, you know? I said, my daddy gave me that name when I was small. Everything I used to see, I used to pick up, so they used to call me Pickup, you know? So, it developed from Pickup into Picky, see? And up until today, the name still sticks with me. I thought it was Pickett. No, Pickett, P-I-C-K-E-Y. Pickett. Oh, I thought it was Pickett, like E-K on it. Yeah. Well, a lot of people, when they call me Pickett, but when they write it down, they write it Pickett, you know? Yeah, that's right. Well, that's what Harold asked me about, Harold Dejean asked me about, uh, asked me my name, then I told him my name. He said, you mean to tell me you Cyclone Johnny's son? I said, that's right. He said, well, that's my cousin, Cyclone Johnny. He said, well, you know Leo Dejean's my brother? And that's how I come to get with Harold Dejean. All right. Now, I got with Harold Dejean, then, uh, I told Harold where I was living and a lot of things, and he said, man, he said, well, I got to come get there for some more jobs. I don't know you could play that good, you know? So, that's what he used to tell me about Leo was strictly reader. He couldn't ad lib at all. You know, he was, he was the first trumpet player for AJP, Ron. Oh, that's right. I didn't know. Yeah. Leo Dejean. He had tone, he had everything a trumpet player need, but he couldn't play an ad lib solo. He couldn't play nothing. Read everything, you know? He said, I'd like to give the job to Leo. He said, well, Leo can't play with these people want out here. Like playing them hunky tongues. See? So, that's where, uh, what I got with him. So, eventually, the time passed by and, uh, and I got with, uh, uh, Harold, Harold got to, to go on his boat, uh, the S.S. Dixie. Yeah, S.S. Dixie. Yeah, S.S. Dixie. Went to New York. Went to New York. Yeah, yeah, that's right. Yeah, S.S. Dixie. The Morgan Line. That's what it was. And, uh, well, he, he, uh, he went to see my dad and got consent to take me to New York and all that. All right. All that was, well, I went to New York. See? And, uh, and I mean, I, well, we was playing on the boat for the passengers. I think we used to play at, uh, at four o'clock in the evening. We used to play about a half an hour. And then at night, we used to play for the passengers about two or three hours, something like that at night. You know, just play real soft. I had to play with a mute all the time. Yeah, see? So, and, and the, and the captain was kind of doubtful about taking me because, I mean, I was so young. See? So, uh, Harold talked to him and he said he got my father's consent and all and a lot of dilly dally. So that's how I come to make the trip. Okay? It was 17 days from here to New York. I mean, I mean, the whole trip, uh, was 17 days, see? So, uh, well, I got with Harold. So Harold found out he used to buy orchestrations. That was all those, that was all a go at that time, orchestrations, see? So Harold, uh, used to buy a lot of orchestration and then he, and he, you know, give me my part, see? And I just take the music and just look at it like that, you know? He say, uh, it looks hard? I say, yeah, man, that's hard, you know? And I say, see? He said, well, I'll tell you what. He said, I'll play the first course and then he said, then probably you could catch on. But I never did tell him, I mean, I couldn't read, you know? Right then and there, see? So, uh, well, eventually he found out for himself. He said, well, boy, you can't read nothing. I said, well, no. You know? He said, well, you mean tell me as well as you could play? He said, you never learned how to read? So I told, even told him who I was playing with when I found out that he was caught himself looking out for me and all that, see? So, uh, well, uh, well, anyhow, uh, well, Harold said, well, look, he said, well, I'm going to see if I can teach you how to read. So I don't know. He called himself teaching how to read, but I never accomplished anything with him. So on a couple of those trips we gone, I think I worked on it both for about eight months. A couple of those trips gone, that's where I first met Fats Pichon in New York City, see? Uh, he was working with another trumpet player from here called Raymond Brown. Yeah, he used to play with Fats Band when Fats Band was here, okay? So, uh, uh, that's where I first met Pichon was in New York, see? So, uh, uh, Fats was having a kind of rough up there, you know? I mean, jobs were scarce and all that. So he said, man, he said, he was telling Harold, you know, he introduced me and all that. Well, he didn't think nothing about me. So, uh, he was telling Harold, uh, about how things was rough and all that. So he told Harold, he said, well, Harold, he said, I think I'm a, I'm gonna go down home, see, after a while, you know? See? So, uh, well, he came on down home and, uh, no, uh, before he left, well, I got to be, uh, which one? You want to close that one? No, it's fine. No, it's fine. Yeah, how about a soft drink now, partner?
Maybe, yeah, if you want to. What kind you want?

Yeah, I gotta, I gotta tell about when I've been, when I've been on the road when I was going to college, you know? And, and I'm in the states I visit. Matter of fact, I mean, I've visited 40, let's see, well, now they got 50 states. I mean, I've, I've visited, when they had 48 states, I visited 45 states out of the 40 when I was going to college, playing the college band. But then, I mean, we'll get to that. Yeah. Uh, well, anyway, I mean, I met Fass Pichon in, in, uh, in New York. So, constantly going by his apartment, going by his apartment, that I, he and I become, be friends, you know? So, Harold DeJong told him I couldn't read. He said, he couldn't read? He said, well, I'll, I'll take him over. He said, wait till we get down home. See? All right. Fass come home, and, uh, so every time we come back to New Orleans, well, I used to go by Fass House, see? So, uh, well, Fass was talking about making up a band, see? I think it was to go on a steamer capital. That, uh, so, uh, well, anyhow, uh, Fass came, uh, that is, I used to go by Fass House every trip. So, eventually, the trips on the boat cut out, you know? Captain said, well, no more music. I don't know why. So, uh, but then I used to go by Fass House, and Fass was making up his band, so he asked me if I wanted to play. I told him, yeah. Well, at that time, I had a wonderful lip. I mean, I used to play all those high notes like Louis Armstrong was playing, and that's what, I think, interests him in me, in taking me. You understand? Because, look, it seemed as though, he had a band before, and, I mean, he had trumpet players, but the things he wanted to write, they couldn't play it. Because I remember, there was one piece he wrote, I don't know if he wrote especially for me, or just what, why he did that, but he used to, uh, uh, I'll always be in love with you, is the name of the tune. And I start off on a high F. I used to make that by myself. You know, you used to knock off one, two, and then the band coming, you know? And I don't know if you want to try me out, or just what you want, or if you wrote especially for me, but it looked like when I used to do that, I mean, I used to bust them notes out there, you know? And I was so young, see? So, it looked like, I guess he must have took interest in me, see? So, uh, well, then he started making up his band, and, and everything like that, so, uh, then he found out, he said, well, you still can't read, and I said, no, I can't read. So, what he used to do, he had a couple of jobs to play, and he wanted me to play the jobs, see? He said, now look, you know what I'm gonna do? He said, now, he used to rehearse in the front room on Claiborne and, uh, Columbus. They got a garage, they got a, some kind of tractor station there now, Claiborne and Columbus. Well, his mother used to own that house, and his mother was a midwife, see? Yeah, see? So, he used to sit down in that section and play those parts, those first parts, and honest to God, I used to remember from the first note in the introduction to the last note, and I had that music in front of me, I couldn't read, wouldn't read no more, and the man in the moon, but I remember it, and hit everything on the head, you know? So, I mean, well, all that impressed, I guess it must have impressed him, I don't know, you know? So, that's where, uh, we went on a boat. He got the job for the steamer captain. River. Yeah, yeah, steamer captain on the river, there, see? But, uh, Captain Roy Streckles, he was the captain of that boat. So, uh, And about what year that was? That was in 1938. Mm-hmm. That was in 1938, when I first got with him then, see? So, uh, let me see. Yeah, so, we went on a boat, and on them trips, you know, he used to take me every day and teach me. Music got five lines and four spaces, and then the notes on the line is EGBD and F, and then the notes in the spaces is F-A-C-E and so forth. This is a treble clef, this is a bass clef sign, this is common time, this is two-fold time, this is this, and this is that, that's the other. And eventually, well, after I caught on to all that, and then, and I began to read, he used to write, like, da, da, da, da, da, da, da, da, da, used to write them kind of things so I could read them instead of me hearing them. You understand? And I mean, he took me off from the very beginning. Now, when I got that I could read good, you know, then I told him, I said, well, Walter said, uh, I want to learn how to arrange. See? And I mean, he took a life with me like that. So he said, well, all right. He said, well, I'll teach you how to arrange. And we, and he learned how I took a three-year course and a year and a half on that boat in arranging. That's right, from, from Pigeon. Well, I mean, I was young, I was single, I had no worries at all. I was making 25 hours a week, which was a big salary at that time. You understand? Yeah. See? So I was making 25 hours a week on a boat in the steam of capital in 1938. I mean, I was planning money. See? So, uh, but that's where, I mean, he learned me how to arrange. Then sometime he and I used to sit down and get together. I used to take numbers off the record. I think I was 16 years old. And I used to take numbers off the record like any professional would do today. See? Well, I mean, I was ambitious and all that. Do you understand? I mean, nothing, I didn't see nothing else but music at that time. See? I even used to play the piano and all that. See? Which, I mean, I still fool around with the piano a little bit. Yeah. See? So, uh, well, let me see. Well, yeah. Well, I mean, I took this three, three-year course in a year and a half with Pigeon. Because matter of fact, like, uh, sometime me and he used to be wrestling, you know, and he'd give me something to study. See? And I mean, I didn't, well, he was older than I was and I was young and full of pep and ambitious. Well, I mean, I ain't had time to go lay down and rest. I'm on the line. You know? See? So, he would, uh, so he would, uh, he would, uh, uh, say, oh boy, look, I'm wrestling now, you know? So, I'd say, well, all right. I mean, if you're wrestling fast, you know, that would be, see? But, in other words, well, you know, I think fast was, he was about in his early thirties. He was about 31, 32 years old or something like that at that time, you know? See? Well, I mean, I was a 16 years old boy, I mean, you know? See, I was very ambitious, you know? Sometimes, like the boat be traveling in the daytime or so like that, going from town to town, you know? And, uh, well, like, say, after we eat lunch or something, we lay down and rest or something like that. Well, at that time, I mean, I was studying, you know? I wasn't thinking about all done, wrestling and all that. See? So, I used to worry him. Did he charge you for lessons? No charge at all. He didn't charge me a nickel. Right. Up until today. And, and that's why, I mean, I give him that, I give him that credit. You know? That's right. That fast P. Shawn, man, he was, he's wonderful. Did you have a place to practice on the boat? Well, on the boat, you practice every day. You had to practice. It was a compulsory in a contract. I don't know if it was in a contract. The whole band. The whole band from 10 o'clock in the morning to 12 o'clock. Every day you had to practice. When the boat was in, in New Orleans, a station in New Orleans, and we used to play it just at night like that, we used to have to go from our house to the boat and practice at 10 o'clock to 12 o'clock. Every morning and every day. I don't know if that was in a contract or if that was day custom or just what it was. Rehorsal every day. And we used to play those day trips that start off at seven o'clock in the morning and end up at 12 o'clock at night for three months. Every day. That's right. I mean, and P. Shawn used to have those arrangements and those stocks. And at that time, Count Basie was just starting out and he was very famous. You see, that's when he had Gordon Dexter with him and the Prez who just died there. Lester Young, they were youngsters and they just thought they were blowing up the storm, you know. So they were very popular. So he used to get a lot of these stocks, stock arrangements and we used to play that. I mean, I really must say, I had iron lip at that time. Never get tired. You make all those iron notes all day and all night and all that, you know. Yeah, it was a real picnic like on a boat, you know. It was it was wonderful, man. I'm telling you. But I don't know. I think I could make that now, you know. Give me a glass, man.
I don't know where I got a glass.
Well, I mean, did you practice on your own as well? A part of the band practice?
Very seldom. Very seldom. I mean, I...
Just as always the band.
Yeah, always was with the band. You see, at some time, or rather on a boat, maybe some guys would feel like practicing. You understand? So, uh...
Huh? I want to... Give me about a half a glass or something. When you did practice by yourself, what did you practice? Scales or long notes?

No. No, I didn't practice no scales. I didn't practice no long notes or nothing. I mean, I used to practice to play more, you know. I mean, to play more solos. Yeah. Because, uh, uh, solos were the thing at that time, you know. See? To play the solos, you know. See? So, in other words, I mean, that's how you were rated with the public. Yeah, that's good. That's how you was rated with the public is with the solos, you know. That's it. Of course, I mean, well, at that time, I mean, I was... I could read like that, you know. So, I mean, I probably wasn't reading anymore. See? My problem was when I do practice, I mean, practice some new ideas or something in solo way. See? So, some of the guys used to play, uh, used to practice their horn like that on a boat when the boat be going from town to town. So, uh, well, then some of the deckhands on the boat and all that, they be, some of them be resting or so like that, and then they complain to the captain about them boys, just to have them. Oh, no, we're getting a chance. Yeah, yeah.
Uh-uh, that's okay. All right, thank you. Give me a minute. Cigarettes.

Got the cigarettes? Got the cigarettes? Did you buy my cigarettes? Mm-hmm. Oh. Well, it's not on the thing, on the top of the thing. So, uh, Bill? Do you want my name, Jeff? No, thank you. I mean, uh, hi, Evan. Yeah. So, uh, well, these deckhands used to complain to the captain, see? So, the captain cut that out. The captain told Pichon, don't leave these musicians practice at all because they disturbed the deckhands and all that. He said, as long as you practice from 10 o'clock to 12 o'clock in the daytime. Well, that was it. And then nobody, no individual practicing at all. And that had to be down in the, on the dance floor of the, of the boat, you know? Well, I stayed on that boat with Pichon for four years. 38, 39, 40, 41. That's how long I stayed on that boat with, uh, with Pichon.
And, uh, now,
let me see, uh, something else I want to talk about. Uh, uh, uh, yeah, well, on the, on the same boat, Fate Marble played on there. P. Ron played on there. You remember, uh, uh, Papa Joe?
No, I don't think so.

Papa Joe, uh, I can't call his last name. He was a trumpet player with Louis Armstrong when Louis Armstrong was on that boat. Joe Howard. Joe Howard. Joe Howard. Yeah. Because I played in the WPN with him. Yeah.
With him. And then they called him Papa Joe.

Papa Joe. Yeah. Yeah. He used to call him Papa Joe. Yeah. So, uh, well, he used to play, because as a matter of fact, I remember him, uh, showing me a picture of him and Louis Armstrong together on, on that boat. I think they got a picture in the union office. Oh. Yeah. Yeah. We just gave a picture. Yeah. Uh huh. Yeah. Papa Joe.
Were you in the WPA band?

No. Yes. That's what I was getting ready to come to. I thought it was something. Well, after we left the boat, then I got in the WPA band. Now, I wouldn't get it. That must have been in 41. In 41 or early part of 42. But I think it was in the late part of 41, around November, December. It might have been January of 42 or February. I know it was cold, see. Well, matter of fact, there wasn't I, nobody else in the WPA band. So, uh, well, I always was, I mean, I was still young. Of course, I got married then. See, I got married in 39, 1939, November, 39. And, uh, and I mean, I was always willing to keep my lip up. See, I even, even after we left the boat, see. So, uh, I don't know. There was some kind of controversy, I mean, that caused us to leave that boat, see, with the band and Pichon, you know. It seems as though, I mean, fast were very popular around New Orleans at that time, because dance bands were very popular. And I left him for a while, because he didn't have too much work, and I had an opportunity to work with Billy Eckstein. Yeah. So I worked with Billy Eckstein a while, see? And that's when I got, we was playing the Regal Theater in Chicago. And I got sick. All right. You see, uh, well, at that time, young, foolish, and wild. You understand? I had an overcoat, and I had a macknowie on. So what I did, I sent my overcoat back home. Yeah. And I put the mack, kept the macknowie on. The macknowie was a little short overcoat, like, you know? And, uh, walking in the snow, knee deep, and all kind of, um, but whatever, I contact cold in my legs.
Is that where you took, uh, Dizzy Gillespie's place with Billy Eckstein?

That's right. That's right. That's where I took Dizzy Gillespie's place. You see? And that's when I got sick, see? Yeah. That's where, uh, matter of fact, at that time, when we was playing the Regal Theater, Dizzy Gillespie was, they had the first seat in the audience, and, uh, and, uh, Charlie Parker, with Charlie Parker, he was behind, he was behind stage with us. He had cam in our dressing room, you know? And was, uh, talking with us. See? Well, that was, that was when I took, uh, Dizzy Gillespie's place, uh, when I joined, when after I left, uh, uh, J. Mac James band, then I joined, uh, Bill Eckstein's place, and, uh, matter of fact, uh, Bill Eckstein, uh, not Bill Eckstein, uh, Dizzy Gillespie's been threatening to leave the band, because it was all in one big cahoot, you know? Like, uh, like the manager said, well, we could put him on, leave him going, he's on, and he could make more money, you understand? Take this guy out. You know, just something like Benny Goodman did. Yeah. You understand? With Lionel Hampton, and, uh, Harry James, and Gene Crouper and them fellas, you understand? Took them out Benny Goodman's band and formed bands behind them, and then there's more money he'd make. Well, that's the same thing that this guy did, see? Well, at that time, well, that was during the war, too. See? Uh, I think it was right after the war, when I joined the band, somewhere around 46, see? 45 or 46, somewhere around in there. And, uh, well, there still was a shortage of musicians, you understand? Sure. See? So that's why he stayed in the band long enough until he could find somebody, and when I got this break to, to, to leave Mac Shandler, then I joined him, see? But then, I mean, well, everything was all right, you understand? Well, that's when they started building up Dizzy Gillespie and Charlie Parker, see? They started off with, with those two, and then, uh, then eventually they branched those two out.
Parker had been in the band, too, as Billy Eckstein did.

Oh, yeah, very, very definitely. Him and, uh, him and Dizzy Gillespie. That's what I taught him. Yeah, both of them in the band together, see? Well, I got sick, and that's why I came back home. And, pfft, I walked on crutches for about two years and seven months. That's bad.
That's right.

That's, that's bad. As a matter of fact, I stayed in bed. How long did I stay in bed? One year. One year. I stayed in bed. That's right. So, uh, then when I did get up. But where I was living at, on Village Street, they used to have old piano in the hall. And as I, I'd hippity hop from the front to the back, I used to play up by that piano, and every time I passed by, I used to bang on it. You understand? Yeah. Well, matter of fact, I couldn't play piano at that time, but I used to, I used to go play a couple of chords from me and learn how to arrange. Well, I used to play those chords, going to, and every time I'd go up and when I'd be coming back towards the room, I'd stop and bang again. So, eventually, I did that so often, until, I mean, well, since one guy went to hire me to play a job playing the piano, he couldn't find nobody else. So, I said, well, yeah, I played it. Walk out there on my crutches, and, and that's how I come to start playing piano. Well, I played piano. Matter of fact, I was, I started off, I think it was at the Dewdrop.
Yeah.
Yeah, Frank Pena's place. I started playing piano there with Buddy Charles and, and, and Papa John. Remember Papa John played bass?
No, I can't remember.
Yeah.
What was his full name?
Uh, uh. Maybe I know him, too. Yeah, you know him. Or, Kaiser's brother. Yeah, we are, sure. Uh, John Joseph. John Joseph, yeah.
Yeah, they call him Papa John.

Yeah, Papa John, that's right. Yeah, John Joseph, you see? Yeah, sure, I know him, yeah. Yeah, see? So, uh, played with John Joseph, and Buddy Charles was playing guitar. We had a trio. And Papa John was old at that time, so, you know, he's still old. He's very old now. So, uh, but then after I left the, left the Dewdrop, I worked there about a year playing piano, maybe better than a year. I was playing piano, but then I got to be pretty good at it, you know? Uh-huh. Then we went at another place on Claiborne Street. Oh, I forgot the name of the place. I was playing piano. I mean, we played there a while. Then, uh, somebody heard that they needed, they wanted a trio in the French quarters. That's why we went at the, at the, the same place, the Shore Bar.
Yeah.

For Frank Ferrari. So, well, he didn't think much of the idea of hiring a trio, so he, I guess he said, well, I think I'll give him something to do anyhow. So, he wanted to see how eager we was to, to, to hold a job. You understand? Yeah. He thought maybe we'd just go there for food. He said, well, I'll tell you what to do. He said, if you want the job, he said, your job start at 12 o'clock at night, you play at 6 o'clock in the morning. I said, well, all right, we take the job. And we did that for about three months. So, he said, well, these fellas really must want to work, you know? So then, I mean, well, he got kind of close with us, and then he found out that we were a family man, you know? And we, and we, we had to work. I mean, we weren't these adventurous type fellas, you know? So, well, we played, we worked there, then we moved next door to the Three Deucers. That was also his place. And I stayed there three years. See? Three Deucers, and that's how I come to Billy's house. See? Off the Three Deucers. Well, then eventually, well, then the Dixieland bands were starting to come in then. You know, that was around 1950, 49. Dixieland band was just starting to come back in. See, Sharky was very famous then at the famous door. See? So, this happened around 1954 or something like that. I couldn't find nothing to do then. I was out of work, you know? And I couldn't find anything to do. I mean, I was having it kind of rough, because my brother-in-law taught me how to paint, and then the paint work was rough, too. See? So, he encouraged me to pick up the trumpet, because Paul Bobrand didn't need a trumpet player. So, I said, oh, man, no, I never make trumpet. He said, man, I'm telling you. He said, man, I played a job last night. Look at the job. Now, he was telling me a story, but he was telling me that to encourage me. He said, man, look at the job paid for $22, man. We played three hours. Look at that, man. Then he pulled out the money and he showed me. You understand? But he was exaggerating, but at that time, I didn't know it. See? He was doing that to encourage me to get back on the trumpet. See? My brother-in-law, that's the son of the head. Brother-in-law, that's the son of the head. So, well, eventually, he keep talking to me. So, I said, well, I don't know the tunes. He said, well, I'll hum the tunes. And I was sitting out right in that chair where you were sitting that day, right on the table there, and I'd take that trumpet, and he'd hum the tune, and I'd play the notes and everything, and get the division and sit down and wrote all them Dixieland tunes out. And I have them inside right now. See? And wrote all them tunes out. Then, eventually, I got with Paul Barbera. See? So, Paul Hyman. So, I stayed with Paul from 54 until 58 of December. That's four years I stayed with Paul. See? Well, we've been to New York, and we've been to California. Paul, we played, uh, in New York, we played, uh, Paramount, wasn't it?
Paramount, yeah. Paramount. We have about ten seconds here to go. Then you joined Bill Matthews.
Then I joined Bill Matthews in December of 1959, and I'm with Bill up until today. .

segments.title: Opening and name
segments.summary: Brunious gives his name; sound check.

segments.title: Willie Humphrey, first teacher, and the Morris Special trumpet
segments.summary: Brunious says Willie Humphrey was his first teacher; he bought a $60 Morris Special trumpet and describes group lessons in a basement.

segments.title: Quitting the horn after his grandfather's death; Professor Milton and learning by ear
segments.summary: He put the trumpet away after his grandfather died, found it dusty, took lessons from Professor Milton but got by copying records and playing by ear.

segments.title: First jobs and playing with older men like Gassum
segments.summary: He cannot recall his first job but played with older men, including a banjoist Gassum's band at 12 or 13.

segments.title: Favorite trumpeter Roy Eldridge and Dizzy Gillespie
segments.summary: Roy Eldridge is his favorite trumpeter; he and his son debate Eldridge and Dizzy Gillespie.

segments.title: Decatur Street jobs, Harold Dejean, S.S. Dixie trips, meeting Pichon
segments.summary: He played Decatur Street dives during the Depression and the Gypsy Tea Room with Kid Renee, joined his cousin Harold Dejean, explains his nickname, travels to New York on the S.S. Dixie, and meets Fats Pichon.

segments.chapter: Fats Pichon and the steamer Capitol
segments.title: Joining Fats Pichon's band on the steamer Capitol and learning to read and arrange
segments.summary: Pichon takes him on despite his not reading, teaches him reading and arranging for free on the boat in 1938, with daily band rehearsals and Basie stock arrangements.

segments.chapter: Fats Pichon and the steamer Capitol
segments.title: Practicing on the boat and why he practiced solos
segments.summary: He seldom practiced alone; when he did, he worked on new solo ideas because soloing was how musicians were rated.

segments.chapter: Fats Pichon and the steamer Capitol
segments.title: Captain bans individual practice; four years with Pichon
segments.summary: Deckhands complained, so the captain limited practice to the morning band rehearsal; he stayed with Pichon four years.

segments.chapter: Fats Pichon and the steamer Capitol
segments.title: Papa Joe Howard and Louis Armstrong on the riverboat
segments.summary: He recalls Papa Joe Howard, trumpeter with Louis Armstrong on the boat, who showed him a picture; they later played in the WPA band.

segments.title: Leaving the boat, joining the WPA band, and Pichon versus Robichaux battles of bands
segments.summary: After leaving the boat he joined the WPA band; he also describes serious battles of bands between Pichon and Joe Robichaux at dances.

segments.title: Mary Jack the Bear and Louis Armstrong's account of her
segments.summary: He discusses whether Mary Jack the Bear is still alive, contrary to Armstrong's book, and suggests the interviewers ask Octave Crosby where to find her.

segments.title: Starting young among older musicians
segments.summary: He stresses he started very young, playing with Kid Renee at 13-14, and has a good memory of the old days.

segments.title: WPA dates and playing for servicemen at 1420 Canal Street
segments.summary: He clarifies he joined the WPA band around 1941-42, playing for sailors and soldiers at 1420 Canal Street during the war.

segments.title: How he got into the WPA band through his brother-in-law and Mr. Martinez
segments.summary: Brother-in-law Eddie Johnson brought him to sit in; bandleader Joe Martinez, a classical pianist, helped him get hired.

segments.title: Leading a WPA band and its personnel
segments.summary: He led one of two WPA bands, with Louis Dumaine leading the other; he lists Charlie Love, Manuel Paul and others.

segments.title: Tinsmith trade school at Xavier after the WPA
segments.summary: After the WPA broke up he trained as a tinsmith at Xavier, with Picou teaching the night class, but stayed in music.

segments.title: The Doghouse job with Eddie Johnson and Lester Santiago
segments.summary: His first Bourbon Street job was at the Doghouse, with Eddie Johnson, Lester Santiago, Charlie Sylvester and Rico; the interviewers ask about Santiago.

segments.title: Ballet Club, writing floor-show arrangements, a week with Benny Carter
segments.summary: He worked about two years at the Ballet Club writing floor-show arrangements for $60, briefly left with Benny Carter, then played with Herbert Leary and Desvigne.

segments.title: Sidney Desvigne, Earl Bostic and Desvigne's band
segments.summary: He recalls bands rehearsing in houses, hearing Desvigne's band with Earl Bostic as a boy, and later playing with Desvigne.

segments.title: Desvigne band personnel and instrumentation
segments.summary: He lists the band's players, including Gaudet, Louis Nelson, Thero Purnell, Euston, Cleo and Judge Riley, and describes its size.

segments.title: Desvigne short-changing pay, and Herbert Leary's band
segments.summary: Desvigne would cut each man's pay, explained through the 'see for yourself' saying; Brunious also mentions Herbert Leary's band.

segments.title: His first funeral parade with old man Allen
segments.summary: The first parade he played was a funeral across the river with Red Allen's father, encouraged by his brother-in-law.

segments.title: Hardships of parading and later funerals with John Casimir, Eureka and George Williams
segments.summary: Walking on shells and rocks is harder than the playing and hurts the lip; he later played with Casimir, Eureka and George Williams.

segments.title: Jay McShann and Billy Eckstine, replacing Dizzy Gillespie
segments.summary: He joined McShann in New Orleans, then Eckstine in Chicago, replacing Dizzy Gillespie, with Charlie Parker visiting backstage.

segments.title: Illness, crutches, and learning piano
segments.summary: Sick from the cold at the Regal Theater, he came home, was bedridden and on crutches for years, and began playing piano on a hall piano.

segments.title: Piano trio at the Dew Drop with Buddy Charles and Papa John Joseph
segments.summary: He started playing piano at Frank Painia's Dew Drop in a trio with Buddy Charles and bassist Papa John Joseph.

segments.title: Frank Ferrari's clubs, return to trumpet, and four years with Paul Barbarin
segments.summary: He worked in the French Quarter trio for Ferrari, returned to trumpet as Dixieland revived, and played with Paul Barbarin from 1954 to 1958.

segments.title: Joining Bill Matthews
segments.summary: He joined Bill Matthews in December 1958 (stated as 1959) and is still with him; the tape ends.
